preamble: Jo March has been writing a book of her own for a long time and keeps it in the garret. Her youngest sister Amy was left behind when the others went to the theatre the day before, and has not forgiven it. Jo has decided the quarrel is over.
extract:
There Jo was mistaken, for next day she made a discovery which produced a tempest. Meg, Beth, and Amy were sitting together, late in the afternoon, when Jo burst into the room, looking excited and demanding breathlessly, “Has anyone taken my book?”

Meg and Beth said, “No.” at once, and looked surprised. Amy poked the fire and said nothing. Jo saw her color rise and was down upon her in a minute.

“Amy, you’ve got it!”

“No, I haven’t.”

“You know where it is, then!”

“No, I don’t.”

“That’s a fib!” cried Jo, taking her by the shoulders, and looking fierce enough to frighten a much braver child than Amy.

“It isn’t. I haven’t got it, don’t know where it is now, and don’t care.”

“You know something about it, and you’d better tell at once, or I’ll make you.” And Jo gave her a slight shake.

“Scold as much as you like, you’ll never see your silly old book again,” cried Amy, getting excited in her turn.

“Why not?”

“I burned it up.”

“What! My little book I was so fond of, and worked over, and meant to finish before Father got home? Have you really burned it?” said Jo, turning very pale, while her eyes kindled and her hands clutched Amy nervously.

“Yes, I did! I told you I’d make you pay for being so cross yesterday, and I have, so...”

Amy got no farther, for Jo’s hot temper mastered her, and she shook Amy till her teeth chattered in her head, crying in a passion of grief and anger...

“You wicked, wicked girl! I never can write it again, and I’ll never forgive you as long as I live.”

Meg flew to rescue Amy, and Beth to pacify Jo, but Jo was quite beside herself, and with a parting box on her sister’s ear, she rushed out of the room up to the old sofa in the garret, and finished her fight alone.

When the tea bell rang, Jo appeared, looking so grim and unapproachable that it took all Amy’s courage to say meekly...

“Please forgive me, Jo. I’m very, very sorry.”

“I never shall forgive you,” was Jo’s stern answer, and from that moment she ignored Amy entirely.

As Jo received her good-night kiss, Mrs. March whispered gently, “My dear, don’t let the sun go down upon your anger. Forgive each other, help each other, and begin again tomorrow.”

Jo wanted to lay her head down on that motherly bosom, and cry her grief and anger all away, but tears were an unmanly weakness, and she felt so deeply injured that she really couldn’t quite forgive yet. So she winked hard, shook her head, and said gruffly because Amy was listening, “It was an abominable thing, and she doesn’t deserve to be forgiven.”

With that she marched off to bed, and there was no merry or confidential gossip that night.

“Everybody is so hateful, I’ll ask Laurie to go skating. He is always kind and jolly, and will put me to rights, I know,” said Jo to herself, and off she went.

Amy heard the clash of skates, and looked out with an impatient exclamation.

“There! She promised I should go next time, for this is the last ice we shall have. But it’s no use to ask such a crosspatch to take me.”

“Don’t say that. You were very naughty, and it is hard to forgive the loss of her precious little book, but I think she might do it now, and I guess she will, if you try her at the right minute,” said Meg. “Go after them. Don’t say anything till Jo has got good-natured with Laurie, than take a quiet minute and just kiss her, or do some kind thing, and I’m sure she’ll be friends again with all her heart.”

“I’ll try,” said Amy, for the advice suited her, and after a flurry to get ready, she ran after the friends, who were just disappearing over the hill.

It was not far to the river, but both were ready before Amy reached them. Jo saw her coming, and turned her back. Laurie did not see, for he was carefully skating along the shore, sounding the ice, for a warm spell had preceded the cold snap.

“I’ll go on to the first bend, and see if it’s all right before we begin to race,” Amy heard him say, as he shot away, looking like a young Russian in his fur-trimmed coat and cap.

Jo heard Amy panting after her run, stamping her feet and blowing on her fingers as she tried to put her skates on, but Jo never turned and went slowly zigzagging down the river, taking a bitter, unhappy sort of satisfaction in her sister’s troubles. She had cherished her anger till it grew strong and took possession of her, as evil thoughts and feelings always do unless cast out at once. As Laurie turned the bend, he shouted back...

“Keep near the shore. It isn’t safe in the middle.” Jo heard, but Amy was struggling to her feet and did not catch a word. Jo glanced over her shoulder, and the little demon she was harboring said in her ear...

“No matter whether she heard or not, let her take care of herself.”
editorialCuts: Removed the 180-word paragraph explaining what the book was worth to Jo and how much of it was written, which tells the reader what the scene is about to show.
Removed the paragraph on the family waiting out Jo’s temper, which stands outside the action and comments on it.

Removed the paragraph in which Amy repents at length; her one-line apology carries it. NOTE, because the earlier record got this wrong: this cut also removes the sentence about overtures of peace being repulsed, and two vocabulary targets were still being shipped from it. They have been replaced from the retained text rather than the paragraph restored — a target chosen from the source and left behind by a cut is Addendum 26 running in reverse.

RESTORED Laurie’s "I’ll go on to the first bend" — an internal cut that appeared in no cut list at all and left "As Laurie turned the bend" using a definite article for a bend the extract never introduced. Costs 37 words.

ENDS BEFORE THE ICE BREAKS. The chapter continues into Amy going through the ice and being pulled out. Cut in full: a near-drowning is a distressing turn for a comprehension paper, and the extract loses nothing by stopping on the sentence that is the moral hinge anyway.

contentFlags: Jo shakes Amy until her teeth chatter and boxes her ear. Recommendation: KEEP, with the reason stated. It is the inciting act, it lasts two sentences, the narrator does not endorse it, and the mother corrects it within the extract. This is not the sustained intimidation the bank rejected in the Treasure Island blind-beggar scene.
Amy destroys a year of her sister’s work out of spite. Recommendation: keep; the passage is about the consequence and treats it as serious.
Cut rather than flagged: the near-drowning that follows. See editorialCuts.
curationNotes: Chosen over the ice-breaking scene that follows it, which is the more famous half of the chapter and turns on a child going under the water. The quarrel alone carries a complete arc — offence, retaliation, refusal, and a refusal held past the point where it costs something — and stops on the line where Jo decides not to call out. Chosen over the burnt-manuscript scene in isolation, which has an inciting act and no consequence. BAND: 884 words at RA 10-13 after the restored paragraph, up from 847.

complicationSeparation.description: Jo’s refusal to forgive, spoken flatly at the tea table, against the same refusal acting on her when it has a price.
complicationSeparation.halfBAnchor: let her take care of herself
complicationSeparation.sceneBeatBetween: the night, the mother’s advice, and the walk to the river
complicationSeparation.descriptionIsAKnownHook: KEPT DELIBERATELY, RULED 2026-08-14. This field STATES THE RELATION and therefore hands a drafter the T4 key. That is a fault by the test the Stream-B anchors were built to pass — learn where to look, not what the answer is — and it is NOT being repaired. Removing it would destroy a baseline and change retrospectively what four already-built clusters mean. The divergence is recorded as a controlled comparison instead: see complication_find_rate.py, arm 1. Any NEW Stream-A passage should carry anchors without a description.

narratorialSignposting.closest: the little demon she was harboring said in her ear
narratorialSignposting.reading: That names Jo’s state at one moment; it does not name the method the passage runs on, which is that every refusal is reported as speech or action and never as a decision. Jo is never said to choose anything. The phrase is a strong lead for an item on that line and an author should not build a whole-text T4 on it.

authoringRead.openingReference: FAULT FOUND, FIXED IN THE PREAMBLE. The extract’s first three words are "There Jo was mistaken" — a deictic pointing at a belief held in a paragraph that is outside the extract. A child has nothing to be mistaken about. The preamble now carries it ("Jo has decided the quarrel is over"). Starting one paragraph later would have lost both the discovery and "tempest", a vocabulary target. Every other reference in the first paragraph resolves: Jo, Meg, Beth and Amy are all named in it.
authoringRead.seams: THREE INTERNAL CUTS AFTER THE RESTORE, WALKED IN READING ORDER, AND THE WALK IS WHAT FOUND THE FOURTH. 648->650 drops the paragraph in which Mrs March comes home; the join runs "she rushed out of the room up to the old sofa in the garret, and finished her fight alone." -> "When the tea bell rang, Jo appeared", which carries its own time marker. Sound. 652->654 drops the family-waiting paragraph; the join lands on "As Jo received her good-night kiss, Mrs. March whispered gently", which names Mrs March on her first appearance in the extract rather than relying on the cut one. Sound. 656->658 drops the repentance; the join goes from "she marched off to bed" to Jo proposing to go skating. SOFT AND KEPT: no reference breaks, but the time marker for the new day ("It was bitter cold in the morning") was in the cut paragraph, so nothing but the paragraph break carries the night. An author should not write a when-does-this-happen item there. THE FOURTH, NOW REVERSED: 663->665 dropped Laurie’s "I’ll go on to the first bend", leaving "As Laurie turned the bend" with a definite article and no bend. It was in no cut list, which is why it was never argued about — an undocumented cut is one nobody re-reads. Restored.
authoringRead.pronounResolution: MANDATORY — two of the three remaining cuts remove paragraphs naming people (Mrs March; Aunt March, Meg and Beth). Every paragraph-opening pronoun resolved against the extract alone. The one that needed the check is "she" opening the paragraph after the good-night kiss, which resolves to Jo and not to Mrs March, who spoke last — fixed inside the sentence by "said Jo". Mrs March is named on every appearance she has in the extract, never pronominalised across a cut. Amy and Jo are both named at every seam crossing.
